label: bm-competing-approaches
topic: Competing and complementary approaches to printed passive shape change, and what a sceptical reviewer would say about the Lean-constrained humidity bilayer
summary: Four of the five alternatives are real and measured but none is a drop-in rival to a passive, reversible, humidity-driven element. (1) Shape-memory polymers are far faster and stiffer: Ding 2017 reports transformation in about 20 s with a 1 GPa/1 MPa pair, and a Formlabs Clear resin printed on a Form 2 recovers at 0.306 deg/s with about 5 N force; but both need heat (62 C and 120 C tested) and are one-shot. (2) A thermal bilayer is the same Timoshenko law with a different driver (his 1925 paper is about bimetal thermostats), and stock Formlabs resins already give a large mismatch: Tough 1000 at 161.6-168.2 and Rigid 10K at 41-48 micrometre/m/C, so 0.45-0.51 percent differential strain over 40 K (own calculation), 2.3-2.5 times the 0.2 percent humidity estimate of earlier agents, with a printable thickness ratio (0.29-0.31) and no thin-wall problem; its weaknesses are that Tough 1000 softens at 40-45 C and nobody has measured such a bilayer. Bloom (14,000 thermobimetal tiles on 414 panels) is the built precedent but gives no curvature numbers. (3) Fibre-aligned hydrogels bend through 20-720 degrees in 1-280 minutes in the literature range but are soft (kPa to 100 kPa) and wet-only. (4) Kirigami and auxetics (tracking to +/-1.0 degree, over 300 cycles) are geometries that need an external strain, so they complement rather than replace a bilayer. (5) Snap-through beams act in 0.6-108 s once a swelling threshold is crossed, but the numbers are solvent-triggered. The three hardest objections: (a) the law is a 1925 formula with a 2015-published maximum that over-predicts printed soft bilayers about 4 times, and Lean certifies only the algebra; (b) strain and speed in humid air are unmeasured and the estimated t90 is a day and a half for 0.4 mm; (c) temperature is a bigger and faster driver of these resins than humidity, so the proposal needs a temperature-by-humidity factorial before any claim. Each has an experiment with a pass/fail rule in the findings and recommendations. Confirmed or corrected from earlier agents: Flexible 80A V2 gains 8 percent mass and 3 percent volume in 1 day (contradicts the blanket under-1-percent claim); its hardness drop is 26 not 28 points; the 3/2 ceiling is prior art (Holstov 2015).
lay_summary: The team wants a printed panel that bends by itself when the air gets damp, like a pine cone. We looked for rivals. A plastic that remembers its shape can snap into a curve in about twenty seconds, but only when warmed and only once. Two layers of plastic that expand by different amounts when warm, like the strip in an old thermostat, can be made from the same Formlabs resins the team already plans to use, and our arithmetic says warmth would bend them more than damp air would. Cut-and-fold sheets and snap-through strips can move a lot, but they need something else to push them. A fair critic would say three things: the maths is old and over-promises for soft plastics, nobody has measured how fast or how far these resins swell in damp air, and ordinary heat from the sun may swamp the effect. We lay out one test for each worry, with a pass or fail rule agreed before any panel is printed.

glossary.plain: Two thin layers stuck together that expand by different amounts, so the pair bends like a bimetal strip.
A 1925 formula giving how tightly a two-layer strip curls from the mismatch in swelling and stiffness of its layers.
The curl can never exceed one and a half times the strain mismatch divided by strip thickness, however stiff the layers.
A proof-checking program that confirms a mathematical argument has no gaps.
A plastic that can be bent and frozen in a new shape and then springs back to its first shape when warmed.
The temperature where a hard plastic turns soft and rubbery.
How much a material grows per degree of warming.
A soft, jelly-like plastic that soaks up a lot of water and swells.
Cut-and-fold paper art; a cut sheet that pops into 3D when pulled.
A structure that gets fatter sideways when you stretch it.
A sudden flip of a buckled strip from one curved shape to its mirror image.
How long water takes to soak through a layer until it is 90 percent of the way to full.
The measured curl divided by the largest curl the law allows; 1 means perfect, small means the law over-promises.
A resin 3D printer that cures liquid with light, and a powder 3D printer that melts nylon with a laser.
The temperature at which a plastic bar sags under a standard load.

findings.claim: SMP bilayers print on a commercial multimaterial inkjet machine (not a Formlabs printer) and reach the programmed curved shape within seconds of immersion in 62 C water; this is the strongest measured speed among the alternatives.
findings.evidence_quote: They transformed into their permanent configuration within a few seconds, depending on the specific sample.

findings.claim: In the same paper the whole transformation was complete after about 20 s.
findings.evidence_quote: After ~20 s, the samples had completed the transformation

findings.claim: Stiffness of the SMP/elastomer pair: glassy SMP about 1 GPa, elastomer about 1 MPa. A 1000-fold modulus contrast, with the stiff layer being the thermally-triggered one.
findings.evidence_quote: At room temperature, the SMP is glassy with a modulus of ~1 GPa, which is two to three orders of magnitude stiffer than the elastomer ( E ~ 1 MPa)

findings.claim: Glass transitions of that pair are 62 C (SMP) and 8 C (elastomer), so activation needs a surface hotter than normal ambient; a sun-heated dark facade could reach it but the paper tested only warm-water immersion.
findings.evidence_quote: temperatures of the SMP and elastomer are 62°C and 8°C, respectively

findings.claim: The deployed shape is one-shot: after heating, the curved permanent shape stays largely unchanged on further cooling and heating (reprogramming needs a separate mechanical heat-and-fix step). A passive reversible daily cycle is therefore NOT what this SMP route delivers.
findings.evidence_quote: remains largely unchanged upon further cooling and heating

findings.claim: Authors of the SMP printing paper (Ge 2016) state the speed and stiffness advantage over hydrogels: SMP modulus MPa to GPa and response seconds to minutes, against hydrogels at kPa to 100 kPa and response of tens of minutes to days.
findings.evidence_quote: faster response rates (in the scale of seconds to minutes depending on actuation temperature)

findings.claim: Same paper, hydrogel side of the comparison: hydrogel response is limited by solvent diffusion on a time scale of tens of minutes, hours or days.
findings.evidence_quote: the solvent diffusion based slow response rates in the time scale of a few ten minutes, hours, and even days

findings.claim: Ge 2016 printed methacrylate SMP networks with failure strain above 300 percent on a projection microstereolithography system, a vat-photopolymer route like Formlabs SLA but a research machine with micron resolution.
findings.evidence_quote: failure strain which is more than 300% and larger than any existing printable materials

findings.claim: A Formlabs vat printer HAS been used for shape memory: Clear resin (named FLGPCL02) printed on a Form 2, 6 x 19 x 115 mm bars, programmed and recovered at 120 C. Average recovery speed was 0.306 deg/s at 0.1 mm layers and 0.308 deg/s at 0.025 mm layers.
findings.evidence_quote: The average recovery speed for the samples with 0.1 mm layer thickness was calculated at 0.306 degrees/second

findings.claim: Recovery force of those Formlabs Clear SMP bars: 5.34 N (0.025 mm layers) and 4.76 N (0.1 mm layers), a 4.5 to 5.8 N range across print orientations.
findings.evidence_quote: The average recovery force for samples with 0.025mm layer thickness was calculated as 5.34 N

findings.claim: Own arithmetic: at 0.306 deg/s a 90 degree programmed bend takes about 294 s (90/0.306) to recover, but only at 120 C; the test furnace temperature was well above the glass transition, so the study shows the Formlabs resin is a working SMP, NOT that it can be triggered by a sun-warmed facade. The study does not state the resin Tg.
findings.evidence_quote: the temperature was raised to 120°C (above the glass transition temperature)

findings.claim: The bimetal law and the humidity-bilayer law are the same law: the formula the project calls Timoshenko is from his 1925 bimetal-thermostat paper; the driver changes (thermal mismatch alpha*dT instead of swelling strain) but the Lean-checked ceiling kappa*h/d_eps <= 3/2 applies unchanged with d_eps = delta-alpha * delta-T.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSA.11.000233 (Crossref record: "Analysis of Bi-Metal Thermostats", J. Opt. Soc. Am. 1925; text not read, paywalled)

findings.claim: Bloom (Los Angeles, 2011): a built thermobimetal canopy. Its responsive surface is made of 14,000 thermobimetal tiles supported on 414 hyperbolic-paraboloid panels; each tile curls a specified amount above 70 F (21.1 C) or when the sun hits it, no power. The page gives no curl angle, thickness or response time.
findings.evidence_quote: Each individual piece automatically curls a specified amount when the outdoor ambient temperature rises above 70˚F or when the sun penetrates the surface.

findings.claim: Resolving an apparent conflict: earlier-in-session snippets said 14,000 tiles and a review said 414 panels; both are on the same page (14,000 tiles on 414 panels), they are not rival counts.
findings.evidence_quote: Composed of 414 hyperbolic paraboloid-shaped stacked panels

findings.claim: A 2025 review of adaptive shading states the trade-off in general terms: passive smart-material systems are simpler and more sustainable but often lack responsiveness to dynamic conditions.
findings.evidence_quote: passively actuated systems use smart materials that respond to environmental stimuli, offering simpler and more sustainable operation, but often lack responsiveness to dynamic conditions

findings.claim: Formlabs data sheet, Tough 1000: thermal expansion (0-150 C) 161.6 (green) and 168.2 (post-cured) micrometre/m/C; the micro sign is lost in the PDF text extraction and the table columns are scrambled, so the green/post-cured mapping is my reading.

Formlabs data sheet, Rigid 10K: thermal expansion (0-150 C) in the metric column reads 48, 41, 47 and 46 micrometre/m/C across four conditions (mapping scrambled); imperial column 23-27 microinch/in/F, which x1.8 gives 41-49, consistent.

Tough 1000 softens near ambient-plus: heat deflection temperature at 0.45 MPa is 40.4 C (green) and 44.6 C (post-cured). A 20-60 C thermal swing therefore crosses its softening range, so the modulus ratio n (and the optimum thickness ratio) change during the swing and a CTE averaged over 0-150 C probably overstates the glassy-range value.

Own calculation: stock Formlabs pair Tough 1000 (high CTE, soft, active) on Rigid 10K (low CTE, stiff, passive) has a differential CTE of 113.6-127.2 micrometre/m/C, i.e. 0.45-0.51 percent differential strain over a 40 K swing (0.23-0.25 percent over 20 K). At the 3/2 ceiling and h = 1 mm this is kappa = 6.8-7.6 per m (radius 131-147 mm); at h = 0.4 mm and 40 K, 17-19 per m (radius 52-59 mm).

Own calculation: for that pair n = E_passive/E_active = 10-11 GPa / 0.932 GPa = 10.7-11.8, the optimum passive/active thickness ratio is m = n^-1/2 = 0.29-0.31 (e.g. 0.23 mm Rigid 10K on 0.77 mm Tough 1000 for h = 1 mm, both above the 0.2 mm Form 4 wall minimum), and an equal-thickness pair already reaches f = 0.93-0.97 of the 1.5 ceiling. Unlike the humidity pair, the stiff layer is the passive one, which is printable.
findings.source: own calculation: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-competing-approaches/calc.py (output calc_out.json) ; moduli from agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json (not re-fetched)

findings.claim: Confirms and sharpens the earlier agents: the thermal differential strain of this stock pair (0.45-0.51 percent over 40 K) is 2.3-2.5 times the 0.2 percent humidity differential that spec-resin-chemistry.json ESTIMATED for 24 h. The 0.2 percent is itself an estimate, never measured.

Anisotropic-hydrogel route (Gladman 2016): composite hydrogel inks with cellulose fibrils aligned along the print path give localized, programmable anisotropic swelling; flat prints fold into complex 3D shapes on immersion in water, with an inverse-design theory. I could read only the abstract, so no curvature or time numbers.
findings.evidence_quote: we printed composite hydrogel architectures that are encoded with localized, anisotropic swelling behaviour controlled by the alignment of cellulose fibrils along prescribed four-dimensional printing pathways

findings.claim: Hydrogel bilayer actuators across the literature span bending angles of 20-720 degrees with actuation times of 1-280 minutes (review, Figure 2a).
findings.evidence_quote: The bending angle of bilayer actuators can range from 20 to 720° with actuation times varying from 1 to 280 min

findings.claim: Hydrogels are soft (kPa to about 100 kPa per Ge 2016), so a hydrogel on a stiff Formlabs resin is mechanically dead under the Timoshenko law (project record bm-hydrogels.json: f = 0.0000-0.11 at m = 1; not re-derived here). This limits fibre-reinforced hydrogels to wet or very humid use and to elastomer partners.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/srep31110 (PMC4976324, Europe PMC full text) ; agents2/bm-hydrogels.json
findings.evidence_quote: the low modulus of hydrogels ranging from ∼kPa to ∼100 kPa

findings.claim: Anisotropy by aligned fibres can also be printed in silicone: PDMS with 15 vol percent glass fibres (direct ink writing) swells anisotropically in solvent, and a cellulose-fibril hydrogel does so in water (Jiang 2019).
findings.evidence_quote: Using 3D printable fibrous composites, we fabricate structures with geometries near bifurcation points

findings.claim: Kirigami with a measured outcome: cut thin-film solar cells on a Kapton sheet tilt their facets when stretched, tracking the sun to within +/-1.0 degree of the predicted direction. The motion is a function of applied uniaxial strain, i.e. the cuts are a transformer and need an external driver.
findings.evidence_quote: we show tracking to within ±1.0° of the predicted pointing vector

findings.claim: Same kirigami trackers survived more than 300 cycles without appreciable performance loss, a durability figure that no humidity-bilayer source I read matches (wood: about a dozen loops; printed cellulose: 170 cycles per project record).
findings.evidence_quote: no appreciable decrease in performance after >300 cycles

findings.claim: Conventional trackers raise yearly energy by 20-40 percent over fixed arrays, which is what the kirigami tracker is benchmarked against.
findings.evidence_quote: conventional trackers can provide an increase in yearly energy generation between 20 and 40% compared with non-tracking solar arrays

findings.claim: Buckling-induced kirigami: a perforated sheet under uniaxial tension buckles out of plane into 3D patterns; stretching far leaves permanent folds. Again the input is tension, not humidity. I read the abstract only; no tilt/strain numbers retrieved.
findings.evidence_quote: under uniaxial tension the ligaments buckle out of plane, inducing the formation of 3D patterns whose morphology is controlled by the load direction

findings.claim: Own reading of the kirigami and auxetic literature in this run: kirigami and auxetics are geometries that convert an in-plane strain into out-of-plane motion; I found no source in which one is driven by humidity or temperature alone. They are therefore COMPLEMENTS to a bilayer (strain amplifier) rather than substitutes. Hypothesis, not tested here.

Swelling-triggered snap-through (Jiang 2019): printed fibrous-composite beams near a bistable/monostable boundary snap when anisotropic swelling crosses a bifurcation; actuation time is programmable from 0.6 to 108 s for millimetre-scale structures, with no electronics.
findings.evidence_quote: The actuation time can be programmed by varying structural parameters (from 0.6 to 108 s for millimeter-scale structures)

findings.claim: The snap time quoted above is the time after the trigger crosses a threshold; the slow step is still diffusion. The authors say conventional swelling actuation can take many minutes due to diffusion limits, and the snap gives a fast, large-amplitude output from a slow stimulus.
findings.evidence_quote: This forces a key geometric parameter to pass through a bifurcation, triggering rapid and large-amplitude self-actuation.

findings.claim: Isotropic PDMS in the same paper swells 42 percent linearly in toluene; the glass-fibre composite is the anisotropic one. The 0.6-108 s numbers come from solvent-triggered PDMS/glass-fibre and hydrogel beams, not from humid air.

Prior art for the ceiling: Holstov, Bridgens and Farmer (2015) plotted the Timoshenko factor f(m,n) over many stiffness ratios and wrote that its maximum stays at 1.5, reached at a different thickness ratio each time. The Lean kernel proof is new; the number is not. (Agrees with agents2/bm-wood-cellulose-hygromorphs.json, contradicts spec-hygromorph-4d.json which called it the project's own derivation.)
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)
findings.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

findings.claim: Speed benchmark for a wood humidity bilayer: 1 mm rotary-cut veneer on 0.2 mm fibreglass reached 80 percent of the curvature change in about 2 h 15 min in both directions.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)
findings.evidence_quote: 80% of the total curvature change in both the transfer from dry conditions to humid and vice-versa is achieved in approximately 2 hours 15 minutes

findings.claim: Timoshenko prediction vs measurement in printed soft humidity bilayers (Dingler 2021, PEDOT:PSS on PDMS): measured peak curvature of the 54 micrometre bilayer was about one third of the 17 micrometre one (1.2 per mm).
findings.evidence_quote: A maximum curvature of 1.2 mm –1 was reached, which is about three times the value of the 54 µm bilayer at r.H. = 90%.

findings.claim: Predicted peaks in the same paper: 5.3 per mm for the 17 micrometre film (with humidity-dependent modulus) and 1.6 per mm for the 54 micrometre film. Own arithmetic: 5.3/1.2 = 4.4 and 1.6/(1.2/3) = 4.0, so the formula over-predicts the maximum by about 4 times. The authors themselves say the calculation "nicely predicts the trends", so this is an over-prediction of size, not of shape.
findings.evidence_quote: The maximum curvature predicted from a humidity dependent E PDOT:PSS is 5.3 mm –1

findings.claim: Humidity changes the modulus of the active layer itself: PEDOT:PSS storage modulus fell by a factor of 2.4 from lowest to highest humidity (about 130 to 54 MPa), the reason the law must be fed wet-state, not dry, moduli.
findings.evidence_quote: This leads to a decrease in E' by a factor of 2.4 from lowest to highest humidity.

findings.claim: Dingler et al. name the cause: an inherent linear assumption in the Timoshenko equation, with rotations that become large; they suggest large-rotation beam models or finite elements. (Strictly, curvature from small material strain does not need small rotation, so the stated cause is not the whole story; the humidity-dependence of E and the wide-plate geometry also matter.)
findings.evidence_quote: It has to be noted, however, that there is an inherent linear assumption in the Timoshenko equation.

findings.claim: For filament-printed wood-PLA bilayers, even the extended model could not reproduce observed values because non-linear material behaviour is not in the model (Krueger 2021).
findings.evidence_quote: Although the observed experimental values could not be reproduced computationally, because the potentially non-linear material behavior is not accounted for in the model

findings.claim: Dingler 2021 overall verdict is more favourable than the over-prediction suggests: calculated curvatures follow the experimental trends.
findings.evidence_quote: Overall, the analytically calculated curvatures nicely predict the trends of the experimental actuators.

findings.claim: CONFIRMS bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json and CONTRADICTS the blanket claim in spec-resin-chemistry.json that every SLA resin gains under 1 percent water: Flexible 80A Resin V2 data sheet (ASTM D471 slabs, wiped dry, no conditioning) gives, for deionized water, +8 percent mass and +3 percent volume after 1 day and +9 percent mass and +7 percent volume after 1 week. Column mapping: 12th of 18 solvents (acetone, xylene, IPA, TPM, butyl acetate, ethanol, acetic acid, HCl, NaOH, bleach, H2O2, deionized water ...), values read by position, so confidence is medium.
Volume row of the same table, same column mapping: deionized water +3 percent (1 day) and +7 percent (1 week); the neighbours are H2O2 +6/+9 and isooctane +122/+164.

Hardness row, same mapping: deionized water -26 (1 day) and -27 (1 week) Shore A points. This CONFIRMS the later correction (-26, in bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json) and CONTRADICTS the -28 used in design-biomaterial.json.
Test condition for those numbers: slabs are measured immediately after wiping dry with no conditioning, so the values include surface water and no drying hysteresis is represented.
findings.evidence_quote: Rectangular slabs, used for hardness, mass, and volume change, are evaluated immediately after wiping dry without a conditioning period.

findings.claim: Own arithmetic from that table: 3 percent volume is 0.99 percent isotropic linear swelling after 1 day, 7 percent is 2.28 percent after 1 week (1.03^(1/3) and 1.07^(1/3)). Isotropy is assumed, not measured.

Rigid 10K takes up under 0.1 percent IPA in 24 h (1 cm cube), CONFIRMING the passive-layer claim for that solvent; the water row of the same table is scrambled in the PDF text and I could not read it. I did not re-check the 39 percent IPA figure for Elastic 50A.
findings.evidence_quote: Isopropyl Alcohol < 0.1

findings.claim: Own calculation of one-face-exposed 90 percent equilibration time t90 = 0.848 h^2/D (coefficient from agents2/bm-diffusion-kinetics.json, not re-derived here). With D = 1e-12 m2/s (stock rigid methacrylate resin, earlier agents' literature value, not re-verified): 9 h at 0.2 mm, 38 h at 0.4 mm, 151 h (6 days) at 0.8 mm, 603 h (25 days) at 1.6 mm. With D = 6e-12 (Flexible 80A V2-class, inferred by an earlier agent from Formlabs 1 d/1 wk mass gains): 1.6 h at 0.2 mm, 6.3 h at 0.4 mm, 25 h at 0.8 mm. With D = 1e-10 (hydrogel): 5.7 min at 0.2 mm, 23 min at 0.4 mm, 1.5 h at 0.8 mm.

findings.claim: Own calculation: a 21-fold speed gap between the SMP route and the hydrogel hinge that Ding 2017 uses as comparator (about 20 s versus about 7 min for 36 degrees at 0.8 mm; different geometries and stimuli, so indicative only).
findings.evidence_quote: it takes about 7 min to achieve a bending angle of 36°

findings.claim: Own calculation, arc swept by a strip at the 3/2 ceiling: for d_eps = 0.5 percent, h = 1 mm and L = 100 mm the strip bends through 43 degrees; for d_eps = 1 percent, h = 0.4 mm, L = 100 mm through 215 degrees. Large rotations therefore arise for thin humid strips, which is where Dingler says linear theory strains.

OBJECTION 1 (the model and the novelty). Reviewer: "The proposal rests on a 1925 bimetal formula whose 3/2 maximum was already published in 2015 (Holstov). It over-predicts printed soft humidity bilayers about 4 times (Dingler) or cannot be reproduced at all (Krueger). A Lean proof of an inequality inside that formula says nothing about whether it describes a Formlabs resin, and the Lean file I read proves the bound and equality when m^2 n = 1, not the converse that the optimum is only there." BEST RESPONSE: Concede the novelty claim is narrow (a kernel-checked, assumption-explicit bound), and reframe: the bound is a hard upper filter, it can only err on the side of excluding designs, and an over-prediction means efficiency eta = kappa_measured*h / (1.5*d_eps_measured) is below 1, never above. Report eta and the position of its maximum as the scientific result. The wet modulus, not the dry datasheet value, must set n (Dingler: modulus fell 2.4-fold from 10 to 90 percent RH). Keep the claim to "eta <= 1 and the maximum sits near n_wet^-1/2". EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES IT: Measure d_eps (free swelling strain, coupon of the same thickness as each layer) and wet and dry modulus on single-layer coupons BEFORE printing any bilayer; freeze predictions; print 5 thickness ratios x >=5 strips at fixed total thickness; read curvature in the same bath/chamber. Pass: measured eta within +/-20 percent of f(m,n_wet)/1.5 at every ratio and the argmax within one step of n_wet^-1/2. Falsified if any strip exceeds eta = 1 beyond measurement error (the model or measurement is wrong) or the best strip stays below eta = 0.5 (the law is uninformative for these resins).
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136) ; https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202007982 (PMC11469309) ; https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics6040058 (PMC8544213) ; Lean file D:/Users/ashenoy00000/.antigravity-ide/ScienceClaw/delphisci/tracks/lean/HygromorphCeilingCheck.lean (read only; theorems timoshenkoCoefficient_le, timoshenkoCoefficient_eq_of_optimal, bilayer_rules_out)
findings.evidence_quote: the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

findings.claim: OBJECTION 2 (strain and speed: the physical premise). Reviewer: "No humid-air swelling coefficient or diffusivity exists for any Formlabs resin. Estimates put the differential strain near 0.2 percent per day and the t90 of a 0.4 mm layer at about 38 hours, of 0.8-1.6 mm at 6-25 days. An SMP bilayer moves in seconds, a thermal bilayer in minutes, a snap element in under two minutes, hydrogels in minutes to hours. An architectural element that needs weeks is not an element." BEST RESPONSE: The speed gap is real and cannot be argued away for stock rigid resins; it can be narrowed by design: layers of 0.2 mm (9 h), a Flexible 80A V2-class active layer (D of about 6e-12 gives 1.6 h at 0.2 mm; measured 1 percent linear swelling per day when immersed) or a hydrogel layer (minutes to hours). Slow can be a feature for a seasonal or diurnal element, as with the 2 h 15 min wood hygromorph. State plainly that the two numbers on which everything rests (d_eps in air and D) are unmeasured, and make measuring them the first deliverable. EXPERIMENT: sorption isotherm and kinetics at 23 C, RH steps 30, 60, 90 percent, on 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 mm coupons of Flexible 80A V2, Tough 1000, Rigid 10K, Nylon 11 and Nylon 12 (gravimetry plus optical length to 5 micrometres per 40 mm, plus the same coupon edge-on for curvature when bonded); fit D from the t^0.5 slope. Go/no-go rule written in advance: continue the humidity route only if the differential strain between the best active/passive pair is >= 0.3 percent for 30 to 90 percent RH AND t90 <= 24 h at <= 0.4 mm; otherwise switch to the hydrogel or thermal route.
findings.source: own calculation: D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-competing-approaches/calc.py (output calc_out.json) ; https://media.formlabs.com/asset/af9d9268-d8c4-4019-9ccd-bd3af926c67e/-ENUS-Flexible-80A-V2-TDS.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1602890 (PMC5389747) ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-08055-3 (publisher PDF at raney.seas.upenn.edu) ; https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)

findings.claim: OBJECTION 3 (wrong stimulus and confounding). Reviewer: "Temperature moves these resins more than humidity does. Formlabs' own data give a Tough 1000 / Rigid 10K CTE gap of 114-127 micrometre/m/C, i.e. 0.45-0.51 percent over 40 K against the 0.2 percent humidity estimate, so on a real facade your humidity bilayer will mostly be a thermal bilayer, and a thermal bilayer needs no new material (Bloom is built). Water also plasticises, leaches residual photoinitiator and hydrolyses acrylates, and no humidity-driven shading has a measured energy or comfort benefit." BEST RESPONSE: Accept the physics. The Lean law is driver-agnostic, so restate the proposal as a Lean-bounded bilayer characterised under BOTH drivers, with the thermal response as the control and possibly the better sun-tracking driver (shade is needed when hot). What humidity adds is a stimulus uncorrelated with surface temperature at night and in rain, and the potential to use a bio-based polymer; the case for it is climate-dependent (project record: tracks need for shade in dry-summer cities, fails in humid ones). Durability claims must wait for the cycle and creep data. EXPERIMENT: climate-chamber factorial on identical strips: T = 20, 40, 60 C crossed with RH = 30, 90 percent, with the strip held edge-on, plus 100 humidity cycles and a 7-day creep hold (90 percent RH versus 30 percent). Fit d_eps = delta-alpha*dT + delta-beta*dRH and report each term. Pass for the humidity route: the humidity term is at least half the thermal term over a 20 K daily swing, curvature after 100 cycles is within 10 percent of cycle 1, and mass loss from leaching stays below the swelling signal (dry-wet-dry mass check). Otherwise the honest conclusion is that the thermal bilayer is the better stock-resin design.

key_claims.claim: The Timoshenko 3/2 ceiling is prior art (Holstov 2015 plotted it and wrote that the maximum stays at 1.5); the new element is only the kernel-checked proof, and the Lean file read proves the bound and equality when m^2 n = 1, not the converse.
key_claims.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 (Newcastle open copy of Holstov et al. 2015, doi 10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2015.08.136)
key_claims.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5

key_claims.claim: The formula over-predicts the maximum curvature of printed soft humidity bilayers by about 4 times (5.3 vs 1.2 per mm; 1.6 vs about 0.4 per mm), although it follows trends.
key_claims.evidence_quote: A maximum curvature of 1.2 mm –1 was reached, which is about three times the value of the 54 µm bilayer at r.H. = 90%.

key_claims.claim: Stock Formlabs resins give a larger and faster-driven thermal bilayer mismatch than the estimated humidity one: Tough 1000 CTE 161.6-168.2 vs Rigid 10K 41-48 um/m/C is 0.45-0.51 % over 40 K (own calculation), against 0.2 % estimated for humidity; so a temperature-by-humidity factorial is required before any humidity claim.
The strongest alternatives are faster but not drop-in: SMP bilayers move in about 20 s but need heat and are one-shot; kirigami needs external strain; hydrogel bilayers need 1-280 min and are soft.
key_claims.evidence_quote: They transformed into their permanent configuration within a few seconds, depending on the specific sample.

recommendations: Run the three experiments in the findings (OBJECTION 1-3) in this order: coupon sorption/CTE/modulus first (objection 2 and the inputs for 1), then the T x RH factorial (objection 3), then the bilayer thickness-ratio sweep (objection 1). Write the pass/fail thresholds into the pre-registration before any bilayer is printed.

Add a thermal-only control (20-60 C at fixed RH) to EVERY humidity test; without it a humidity result on these resins is uninterpretable because thermal strain is of the same size or larger (0.45-0.51 % per 40 K vs the 0.2 % estimate).

Print a stock-resin thermal bilayer as a cheap second arm: Tough 1000 (about 0.77 mm) on Rigid 10K (about 0.23 mm) at h = 1 mm; measure curvature versus temperature 20-60 C. It needs no Open Material Mode, tests the Lean ceiling with a driver that is fast, and is the fallback if the humidity go/no-go fails. Check first that the two parts bond (no bond data in any source read).

Treat SMP as an assembly or deployment feature, not as the daily actuator: a Formlabs Clear flat print that is heated and programmed once could be a one-shot deployable pavilion element. Do not claim passive operation without finding or tuning a resin with Tg inside the facade surface range (not found for any Formlabs resin in this run).

Report efficiency eta = kappa_measured*h/(1.5*d_eps_measured) and the thickness ratio of its maximum for every bilayer, wet-state modulus included; state in the proposal that the 3/2 number is prior art (Holstov 2015) and the contribution is the machine-checked bound plus the printer-constraint filter.
Keep kirigami and snap-through as strain-amplifier ideas only after a bilayer gives measured strain; do not claim them as humidity-driven.
